body_html:
Taking a taxi in Spanish is one of the first real conversations most travelers have. The exchange is short, but the details matter: giving the address clearly, agreeing on the price or checking the meter, telling the driver where to stop and paying. In Mexico, ride apps like Uber and DiDi are common, and official airport taxis use prepaid tickets. Here are the phrases for each step, along with the safety habits that locals use.

Quick answer
  • Start: Buenas tardes. ¿Me lleva a la calle Madero, número 20?
  • Price: ¿Cuánto me cobra al aeropuerto? ¿Usa taxímetro?
  • On the way: Siga derecho. Aquí a la derecha.
  • Stop: Aquí está bien, gracias. Déjeme en la esquina.
{{toc}}

Taking a taxi in Spanish: getting in

SpanishEnglish
¿Está libre?Are you free?
¿Me lleva al centro, por favor?Could you take me downtown, please?
A esta dirección, por favor.To this address, please. (showing your phone)
Voy a la calle Juárez, número 45.I’m going to 45 Juárez Street.
Al aeropuerto, terminal 2.To the airport, terminal 2.
¿Sabe dónde queda?Do you know where it is?

Spanish addresses put the street first and the number after: calle Juárez 45. In Mexico, you will also hear colonia for the neighborhood: en la colonia Roma. Giving the neighborhood helps the driver a lot.

Asking about the fare

  • ¿Cuánto me cobra a…? How much do you charge to…?
  • ¿Usa taxímetro? Do you use the meter?
  • ¿Cuánto es más o menos? About how much is it?
  • ¿Acepta tarjeta? Do you take cards?
  • ¿Tiene cambio de quinientos? Do you have change for five hundred?

Some taxis in Mexico don’t use a meter, so agree on the price before you get in. At major airports, buy a ticket at the official taxi counter (taxi autorizado) inside the terminal. In Spain, taxis use a meter by law, and airport trips to the city center often have a fixed fare.

{{image:2}}

Giving directions to the driver

SpanishEnglish
Siga derecho.Keep going straight.
Aquí a la derecha.Right here, to the right.
En el siguiente semáforo a la izquierda.Left at the next traffic light.
Es después del puente.It’s after the bridge.
Más adelante.A bit farther.
¿Puede ir más despacio?Could you go more slowly?
¿Puede esperarme cinco minutos?Could you wait for me for five minutes?

For more direction words, see {{link:asking-for-directions-in-spanish|asking for directions in Spanish}}.

Stopping and paying

  • Aquí está bien, gracias. Here is fine, thanks.
  • Déjeme en la esquina, por favor. Drop me at the corner, please.
  • ¿Cuánto le debo? How much do I owe you?
  • Quédese con el cambio. Keep the change.
  • ¿Me da un recibo? Could I have a receipt?

Tipping taxi drivers isn’t expected in Mexico, though rounding up is appreciated, especially if the driver helps with luggage. In ride apps, you can tip in the app.

{{book:a-road-in-bloom}}

Ride apps

With Uber, DiDi or Cabify, most of the conversation happens in the app, but a few phrases help:

  • Hola, ¿es para Ana? Hi, is this for Ana? (the driver checking)
  • Ya estoy afuera, con chamarra roja. I’m outside now, in a red jacket.
  • Estoy en la entrada principal. I’m at the main entrance.
  • ¿Puede abrir la cajuela? Could you open the trunk? (Spain: el maletero)
  • ¿Puede poner el aire, por favor? Could you turn on the air conditioning, please?

Drivers sometimes call or text before arriving. If you prefer to write, a message like Voy saliendo, dos minutos (Coming out now, two minutes) is perfect. See {{link:texting-in-spanish|texting in Spanish}}.

A sample taxi ride

Tú: Buenas noches. ¿Me lleva a la colonia Condesa?
Good evening. Could you take me to the Condesa neighborhood?

Taxista: Claro. ¿A qué calle?
Sure. Which street?

Tú: A Ámsterdam, casi esquina con Michoacán. ¿Cuánto me cobra?
Ámsterdam, near the corner with Michoacán. How much will it be?

Taxista: Son ciento veinte.
It’s a hundred and twenty.

Tú: Está bien. … Aquí está bien, gracias. Quédese con el cambio.
Okay. … Right here is fine, thanks. Keep the change.

Casi esquina con (near the corner with) is a very common way to give an address in Mexico.

{{image:3}}

Safety tips and common mistakes

  • Use official taxis or apps, especially at night. Ask your hotel: ¿Me puede pedir un taxi seguro?
  • Share your trip with a friend using the app’s share feature.
  • ¿Cuánto cuesta para el aeropuerto? Use a or al: ¿Cuánto me cobra al aeropuerto?
  • Para aquí. Understandable, but blunt. Aquí está bien, gracias is friendlier.

If something goes wrong, see {{link:emergency-phrases-in-spanish|emergency phrases in Spanish}}. Mexico City’s government publishes information on authorized taxis on its SEMOVI transport site.

{{quiz}}

Final thoughts

Taking a taxi in Spanish is a short conversation with a clear script: address, price, directions, stop, pay. Practice the address format and the polite stop phrase, use official taxis or apps, and every ride becomes a small, confident Spanish lesson. For more travel and everyday moments, see {{link:spanish-phrases-for-everyday-situations|Spanish phrases for everyday situations}}.

faq.q: How do you tell a taxi driver where to go in Spanish?
faq.a: Say ¿Me lleva a…, por favor? followed by the address, or show the address on your phone and say A esta dirección, por favor.

faq.q: How do I ask how much a taxi costs in Spanish?
faq.a: ¿Cuánto me cobra a…? or ¿Cuánto es más o menos?

faq.q: Do you tip taxi drivers in Mexico?
faq.a: It isn’t expected, but rounding up or adding a little for help with luggage is appreciated.

faq.q: Are ride apps common in Mexico?
faq.a: Yes. Uber and DiDi are widely used in Mexican cities.
